choices: Increase the CloudWatch alarm period to 1 hour
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the metric with an SNS notification
evidence:
Metric: CPUUtilization > 90%
for 3 datapoints.
Current: nobody is notified.
scenarios.hint: Which two services combine for metric-threshold alerting?
scenarios.situation: An EC2 fleet's CPU exceeds 90% repeatedly, but nobody finds out until users complain.
scenarios.title: Nobody knew the CPU was pegged
scenarios.why: A CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric triggers an SNS notification when the threshold breaches — the standard metric-alerting pattern. Longer periods delay detection; billing dashboards don't monitor CPU; Flow Logs capture network traffic, not CPU.

choices: Enable CloudTrail in all regions with log file validation, delivered to a locked-down S3 bucket
Rely on the console's event history (90 days)
Ask developers to log API calls in the app
evidence:
Requirement: immutable record of
who called which API, when, from where.
Retention: 1 year.
scenarios.hint: Which service exists specifically to log AWS API activity?
scenarios.prompt: Which design meets the audit requirement?
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires an immutable one-year record of every AWS API call: who, what, when, from where.
scenarios.title: Who called what, when
scenarios.why: CloudTrail logs AWS API activity; enabling it in all regions with log file validation into a restricted S3 bucket gives a tamper-evident audit trail. Console event history is only 90 days and not immutable; app-level logging misses console/CLI calls.

choices: The CloudWatch agent for memory and disk metrics
evidence:
Outage: /var filled up.
CloudWatch showed CPU/network fine.
No disk or memory metrics existed.
scenarios.hint: Which metrics does EC2 NOT publish by default?
scenarios.prompt: What would have caught the disk-full outage?
scenarios.situation: An outage was caused by a full disk, but CloudWatch only showed CPU and network — no disk or memory metrics existed.
scenarios.title: The metrics you don't get for free
scenarios.why: EC2 publishes hypervisor-visible metrics (CPU, network, disk I/O) by default, but memory and disk-space utilization require the CloudWatch agent installed on the instance. CloudTrail logs API calls; Config tracks configuration changes — neither monitors disk space.

evidence:
10 GB/day of app logs in
CloudWatch Logs. Need: find all
ERROR lines with trace IDs, fast.
scenarios.hint: Which tool queries CloudWatch Logs with a SQL-like language?
scenarios.prompt: Which tool answers the query fastest?
scenarios.situation: 10 GB/day of application logs land in CloudWatch Logs; the team needs to find all ERROR lines with trace IDs quickly.
scenarios.title: Searching 10 GB of logs
scenarios.why: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides an interactive query language purpose-built for searching and aggregating log data at scale. S3 access logs and Flow Logs are different data sources; X-Ray traces requests but doesn't query log text.

evidence:
50+ operational issues/week.
Need: aggregate, deduplicate,
assign, and track to resolution.
scenarios.hint: Which service is the operational 'to-do list' that aggregates OpsItems?
scenarios.prompt: Which service centralizes operational work items?
scenarios.situation: Dozens of operational issues per week need aggregation, deduplication, assignment, and tracking to resolution.
scenarios.title: The ops to-do list
scenarios.why: Systems Manager OpsCenter aggregates operational issues as OpsItems from CloudWatch, Config, and other sources, with deduplication and investigation workflows. CloudWatch/Trail/Config generate signals; OpsCenter manages the work.

choices: A CloudWatch dashboard with key metrics and alarms
evidence:
NOC wants: one screen, fleet health,
error rates, latency, red/green status.
scenarios.hint: Which CloudWatch feature is the single-pane-of-glass?
scenarios.prompt: What gives the NOC its single screen?
scenarios.situation: The NOC wants one screen showing fleet health, error rates, and latency with red/green status.
scenarios.title: One screen for the NOC
scenarios.why: CloudWatch dashboards provide customizable single-pane views of metrics, alarms, and logs. The EC2 console lists instances without health aggregation; Cost Explorer shows spend; Trusted Advisor shows best-practice checks — none is an ops dashboard.

choices: An Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind an ALB
A single instance with an Elastic IP
evidence:
Single EC2 in AZ-a.
AZ-a outage: 3h downtime.
Requirement: survive AZ failure.
scenarios.hint: What replaces failed instances automatically across fault domains?
scenarios.prompt: Which design survives the AZ outage?
scenarios.situation: A single EC2 instance in one AZ caused a 3-hour outage during an AZ event.
scenarios.title: Beyond the single instance
scenarios.why: An Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs behind an ALB replaces unhealthy instances and routes around failed AZs automatically. Bigger single instances still fail with their AZ; Elastic IPs don't add capacity; two instances in one AZ share the same fault domain.

evidence:
DB on single EC2.
Failure: 6h restore from snapshot.
RTO requirement: < 10 min.
scenarios.hint: Which RDS feature fails over automatically in minutes?
scenarios.prompt: Which database design meets the 10-minute RTO?
scenarios.situation: A database on a single EC2 instance took 6 hours to restore from snapshot; the RTO requirement is under 10 minutes.
scenarios.title: Failover in minutes, not hours
scenarios.why: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby and fails over automatically, typically within minutes. Manual replica promotion and snapshot restores can't meet a 10-minute RTO; bigger instances don't add redundancy.

choices: Health checks on the instances only
ALB target group health checks plus Auto Scaling health checks
No health checks; replace on a schedule
evidence:
Instance hung (app dead, OS alive).
ALB kept sending traffic: 500s.
ASG considered it healthy.
scenarios.hint: OS-alive but app-dead — which health check catches that?
scenarios.prompt: Which health-check design catches the hung app?
scenarios.situation: An instance hung with the app dead but the OS alive; the ALB kept sending traffic and Auto Scaling considered it healthy.
scenarios.title: Alive but not healthy
scenarios.why: ALB target group health checks probe the application endpoint (catching app-dead/OS-alive), and Auto Scaling can use ELB health checks to replace such instances. Instance-level checks only verify the OS; DNS checks don't see app state; scheduled replacement is blind.

evidence:
RTO: 15 min. RPO: 5 min.
Budget: moderate.
Threat: region loss.
scenarios.hint: 15-minute RTO rules out restore-from-backup; 5-minute RPO rules out pilot light — what's left?
scenarios.prompt: Which DR strategy fits the RTO/RPO and budget?
scenarios.situation: Region-loss DR needs 15-minute RTO and 5-minute RPO on a moderate budget.
scenarios.title: Fifteen minutes to recover
scenarios.why: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down live copy replicating data (meeting the 5-minute RPO) that scales up within the 15-minute RTO — the cost/RTO sweet spot here. Backup-and-restore and pilot light can't meet these targets; active-active meets them but costs far more.

choices: An SQS queue with a 30-second visibility timeout
An SQS queue with a dead-letter queue and a long visibility timeout
An SNS topic with no queue
evidence:
One malformed message crashes
the worker every time.
Queue backs up; good messages stuck.
scenarios.hint: What isolates repeatedly-failing messages so the queue keeps flowing?
scenarios.prompt: Which design keeps good messages flowing?
scenarios.situation: A single malformed 'poison' message crashes the worker on every retry, blocking the whole queue.
scenarios.title: The poison message
scenarios.why: A dead-letter queue (DLQ) moves messages that fail repeatedly out of the main queue after max receives, so one poison message can't block everything. Visibility timeout alone just delays the next crash; direct calls and SNS-without-queue lose the message or the buffering.

choices: Enable S3 Versioning and Cross-Region Replication
Rely on a single bucket in one region
Use EBS snapshots of the app servers
evidence:
Critical uploads in S3, single region.
Requirement: survive region loss
with version history.
scenarios.hint: Which two S3 features combine durability, history, and geographic redundancy?
scenarios.prompt: Which S3 design meets the requirement?
scenarios.situation: Critical uploads live in one S3 bucket in one region; they must survive region loss with version history.
scenarios.title: Data that survives a region
scenarios.why: S3 Versioning preserves history (protecting against overwrites/deletes) and Cross-Region Replication copies objects to another region for geographic redundancy. A single bucket is a regional fate-share; manual copies miss the RPO; EBS snapshots don't cover S3 data.

evidence:
3 environments diverged.
Nobody knows which console clicks
built staging.
scenarios.hint: Which approach makes infrastructure reviewable, repeatable, and diffable?
scenarios.situation: Three environments have diverged and nobody can reconstruct how staging was built from console clicks.
scenarios.title: ClickOps leaves no trail
scenarios.why: CloudFormation templates make infrastructure code — versioned, reviewable, repeatable — and change sets preview modifications before applying. Console ClickOps is unrepeatable; hardcoded bash scripts are fragile; wiki runbooks drift from reality.

choices: In-place deployment to all servers at once
Rolling deploys with no health checks
evidence:
Fleet: 60 instances.
Requirement: zero downtime,
instant rollback.
scenarios.hint: Which strategy keeps the old fleet live until the new one proves healthy?
scenarios.situation: 60 instances need zero-downtime deploys with instant rollback.
scenarios.title: Zero downtime, instant rollback
scenarios.why: Blue/green with CodeDeploy provisions the new (green) fleet, validates it, then shifts traffic — the old (blue) fleet stays ready for instant rollback. In-place all-at-once maximizes blast radius; manual SCP doesn't scale; rolling without health checks ships bad builds fleet-wide.

choices: Systems Manager Patch Manager with maintenance windows
User data that patches at boot
evidence:
300 instances, mixed OS.
Compliance: patches within 14 days.
Current: ad-hoc SSH, 40% miss.
scenarios.hint: Which service automates patching fleets on a schedule with compliance reporting?
scenarios.situation: 300 mixed-OS instances need patching within 14 days; ad-hoc SSH misses 40%.
scenarios.title: Patching 300 instances
scenarios.why: Patch Manager automates patching across fleets with baselines, maintenance windows, and compliance reporting. Manual SSH doesn't scale; boot-time patching slows every launch; disabling updates is a compliance violation.

choices: Golden AMIs built by EC2 Image Builder in a pipeline
Manual snapshot of a dev laptop
evidence:
Deploys install deps at boot: 25 min.
Config drift between instances.
scenarios.hint: What bakes a tested, versioned image automatically?
scenarios.situation: Boot-time installs take 25 minutes and instances drift from each other.
scenarios.title: Bake, don't install at boot
scenarios.why: EC2 Image Builder automates building, testing, and versioning golden AMIs in a pipeline — fast launches, no drift. Long-lived pets accumulate drift; laptop snapshots aren't reproducible; single-host containers don't address the fleet.

evidence:
200 developers, 40 projects.
Need: devs access only their
project's resources.
scenarios.hint: Which approach scales permissions by attribute instead of by identity?
scenarios.situation: 200 developers across 40 projects; each developer should access only their project's resources.
scenarios.title: Permissions for 200 developers
scenarios.why: ABAC with tags lets one policy grant access based on matching tags (e.g., project tag on user = project tag on resource) — scaling without per-developer roles. Per-developer roles explode administratively; username wildcards are fragile; root for automation is never acceptable.

choices: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (SecureString) or Secrets Manager
evidence:
DB passwords in 30 AMIs.
Rotation requires rebuilding
all images.
scenarios.hint: Which services are built for secrets lifecycle, including rotation?
scenarios.situation: Database passwords baked into 30 AMIs; rotation requires rebuilding every image.
scenarios.title: Secrets don't belong in images
scenarios.why: Parameter Store SecureString or Secrets Manager centralize secrets outside images, with rotation support — no rebuilds needed. Plaintext env vars and shared docs leak; hardcoded AMI secrets are the current failure.

choices: EBS gp3 volumes for the database
EBS io2 for the database; S3 for the media
evidence:
DB: needs 20k IOPS, persists.
Media: 50 TB, served via CDN.
scenarios.hint: Match each workload to its storage class: provisioned IOPS for the DB, object storage for media.
scenarios.situation: A database needs 20k sustained IOPS with persistence; 50 TB of media is served via CDN.
scenarios.title: Right storage for each workload
scenarios.why: io2 provides provisioned IOPS for the database's performance needs while S3 handles massive media storage with CDN integration. gp3 can't sustain 20k IOPS efficiently; instance store is ephemeral; EFS is a file system, not a media origin.

choices: Copy files over the public internet
evidence:
On-prem NAS: 40 TB.
Need: one-time migration to S3,
with checksums and scheduling.
scenarios.hint: Which service is the managed migration tool with validation?
scenarios.situation: A 40 TB on-prem NAS needs a one-time migration to S3 with checksums and scheduling.
scenarios.title: 40 TB, one trip
scenarios.why: DataSync is the managed service for online data transfer to S3/EFS/FSx with scheduling, bandwidth controls, and data validation. Public-internet copies lack validation; Snowcone/Snowball suit offline/petabyte scale, not 40 TB online; FTP to EC2 is manual and fragile.

choices: S3 Lifecycle policies to transition to Glacier
evidence:
Compliance logs: hot 30 days,
warm 90 days, archive 7 years.
Volume: 1 TB/day.
scenarios.hint: Which S3 feature moves objects between classes on a schedule automatically?
scenarios.situation: Compliance logs are hot for 30 days, warm for 90, then archived 7 years, at 1 TB/day.
scenarios.title: Lifecycle of a log file
scenarios.why: S3 Lifecycle policies automatically transition objects between storage classes (and expire them) on age-based rules — zero ongoing effort. Keeping everything in Standard wastes money; manual moves don't scale at 1 TB/day; deletion violates the 7-year retention.

choices: AWS Backup with a backup plan across services
A cron job on one EC2 instance
evidence:
EC2, RDS, EFS, DynamoDB.
Requirement: centralized 3-2-1
policy, 30-day retention.
scenarios.hint: Which service centralizes backup policies across AWS services?
scenarios.situation: EC2, RDS, EFS, and DynamoDB need one centralized backup policy with 30-day retention.
scenarios.title: One backup policy to rule them all
scenarios.why: AWS Backup provides centralized backup plans, scheduling, retention, and cross-region copy across supported services. Per-service manual snapshots fragment policy; cron on EC2 is fragile; Multi-AZ is availability, not backup.

choices: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
evidence:
Windows app needs SMB shares
with AD integration and
Windows ACLs.
scenarios.hint: Which managed file service speaks native SMB with Active Directory integration?
scenarios.situation: A Windows application needs SMB shares with Active Directory integration and Windows ACLs.
scenarios.title: SMB with Active Directory
scenarios.why: FSx for Windows File Server provides native SMB with AD integration and Windows ACLs as a managed service. EBS is block storage; EFS is NFS (Linux-oriented); S3 is object storage without SMB semantics.

choices: S3 with CloudFront OAC and WAF
evidence:
Static marketing site.
Requirement: HTTPS, DDoS protection,
no public S3 access.
scenarios.hint: Which pattern keeps the bucket private while CloudFront serves it?
scenarios.situation: A static marketing site needs HTTPS, DDoS protection, and no public S3 access.
scenarios.title: Static site, locked-down bucket
scenarios.why: CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC) serves the private S3 bucket over HTTPS with Shield Standard DDoS protection built in; WAF adds application-layer filtering. Public S3 website hosting exposes the bucket; EBS/FTP are unnecessary moving parts for static content.

choices: IAM roles for EC2 with instance profiles
evidence:
App on EC2 calls S3/DynamoDB.
Currently: hardcoded access key
in the AMI, rotated never.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanism gives EC2 temporary credentials automatically?
scenarios.situation: An app on EC2 uses a hardcoded access key in the AMI to call S3 and DynamoDB.
scenarios.title: Keys that rotate themselves
scenarios.why: IAM roles with instance profiles give EC2 temporary, automatically-rotated credentials — no keys to manage or leak. Long-term user keys reintroduce the same problem; sharing keys destroys accountability; hardcoded AMI keys are the current failure.

choices: AWS Config rules with automatic remediation (e.g., revoke on non-compliant)
evidence:
Requirement: no security group
open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22.
Current: violations appear weekly.
scenarios.hint: Which service continuously evaluates configuration and can auto-remediate?
scenarios.situation: Security groups open to the world on SSH keep appearing; monthly audits catch them too late.
scenarios.title: Closing port 22, automatically
scenarios.why: AWS Config rules continuously evaluate resource configuration against the desired state and can trigger automatic remediation (e.g., revoke the rule via Lambda/SSM). Manual audits are too slow; CloudTrail records but doesn't evaluate; Trusted Advisor is advisory, not enforcement.

evidence:
Attack: SQL injection probes
and credential stuffing against
the login endpoint.
scenarios.hint: Which service filters HTTP requests at Layer 7?
scenarios.situation: SQL injection probes and credential stuffing hit the login endpoint.
scenarios.title: Filtering the application layer
scenarios.why: AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at Layer 7 with managed rule groups for SQLi, XSS, and bot/credential-stuffing patterns. Shield handles network-layer DDoS; security groups/NACLs filter packets, not HTTP payloads.

choices: A customer managed key (CMK) with key policies and rotation
evidence:
Regulated workload on EBS.
Need: control who can use the key,
audit key use, rotate annually.
scenarios.hint: Which KMS key type gives you policies, rotation, and CloudTrail audit?
scenarios.prompt: Which encryption design meets the requirements?
scenarios.situation: Regulated EBS volumes need customer-controlled key policies, audited key use, and annual rotation.
scenarios.title: Keys you control
scenarios.why: Customer managed keys (CMKs) in KMS provide key policies for access control, automatic rotation, and CloudTrail logging of every use. AWS-managed keys don't offer key policies; SSE-S3 is for S3; no encryption fails compliance.

choices: Enable GuardDuty in all regions with findings sent to Security Hub
evidence:
Need: detect compromised instances,
crypto-mining, unusual API calls.
Team: 2 people.
scenarios.hint: Which service does threat detection so a 2-person team doesn't have to build it?
scenarios.situation: A two-person team needs detection of compromised instances, crypto-mining, and anomalous API calls.
scenarios.title: Threat detection for a tiny team
scenarios.why: GuardDuty provides ML- and threat-intel-based detection across CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS — a managed detective control a small team can actually operate. Antivirus is endpoint-only; manual log review doesn't scale; security groups are preventive, not detective.

choices: AWS IAM Identity Center with MFA enforcement and permission sets
evidence:
50 employees, 12 AWS accounts.
Need: single sign-on, MFA required,
least-privilege per team.
scenarios.hint: Which service is AWS's SSO with permission sets across accounts?
scenarios.situation: 50 employees across 12 AWS accounts need SSO with enforced MFA and least-privilege access per team.
scenarios.title: One login for twelve accounts
scenarios.why: IAM Identity Center provides workforce SSO across accounts with MFA enforcement and permission sets for least privilege. Per-account IAM users multiply management overhead; shared credentials destroy accountability; password policy alone isn't SSO.

choices: An internet gateway in the private subnet
A NAT gateway in a public subnet
evidence:
Private subnet instances need
OS patches (outbound HTTPS).
No inbound from internet allowed.
scenarios.hint: Which gateway gives outbound-only internet access?
scenarios.situation: Private-subnet instances need outbound HTTPS for patches with no inbound internet access.
scenarios.title: Outbound only, please
scenarios.why: A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets private instances initiate outbound connections while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. Internet gateways are bidirectional; VPC peering connects VPCs, not the internet; VPN connects on-premises networks.

evidence:
Workload must call a SaaS API
over private connectivity —
no internet traversal at all.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS feature exposes services privately inside a VPC?
scenarios.prompt: What keeps the traffic off the internet?
scenarios.situation: A workload must reach a third-party SaaS API without any traffic traversing the public internet.
scenarios.title: PrivateLink to the SaaS
scenarios.why: Interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) expose services — AWS or SaaS-provider — as private IPs inside the VPC with no internet traversal. NAT/internet gateways still use the public internet; public IPs violate the requirement.

evidence:
Need: block a malicious IP range
at the subnet boundary, stateless,
before it reaches instances.
scenarios.hint: Stateless + subnet-level = which control?
scenarios.situation: A malicious IP range must be blocked at the subnet boundary, statelessly, before reaching instances.
scenarios.title: Blocking at the subnet edge
scenarios.why: Network ACLs are stateless subnet-level filters — the right tool for blocking IP ranges at the boundary. Security groups are stateful and instance-level; route tables direct traffic; IAM governs API access, not packets.

evidence:
8 VPCs across 3 accounts.
Need: any-to-any connectivity
without N-squared peering.
scenarios.hint: Which service is the hub for multi-VPC, multi-account networks?
scenarios.situation: Eight VPCs across three accounts need any-to-any connectivity without a full peering mesh.
scenarios.title: Eight VPCs, one hub
scenarios.why: Transit Gateway acts as a central hub routing between VPCs and VPN/Direct Connect across accounts — replacing an N-squared peering mesh. VPC peering is pairwise and doesn't scale here; NAT/internet gateways don't interconnect VPCs.

evidence:
On-prem data center to AWS.
Need: private, consistent throughput
for nightly 5 TB syncs.
scenarios.hint: Private + consistent throughput for heavy hybrid traffic = which dedicated connection?
scenarios.situation: Nightly 5 TB syncs between an on-prem data center and AWS need private, consistent throughput.
scenarios.title: Five terabytes a night, privately
scenarios.why: Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent throughput for heavy hybrid workloads. Site-to-Site VPN runs over the public internet with variable throughput; peering is VPC-to-VPC; internet gateways aren't private.

choices: A custom VPC with public/private subnets across 2+ AZs
The default VPC with all defaults
evidence:
New production workload.
Standard: isolate tiers, survive
AZ failure, no default shortcuts.
scenarios.hint: Production VPC design 101: which layout gives tier isolation and AZ resilience?
scenarios.situation: A new production workload needs tier isolation, AZ resilience, and no reliance on default shortcuts.
scenarios.title: Designing the production VPC
scenarios.why: A custom VPC with public subnets (load balancers, NAT) and private subnets (app, data) across 2+ AZs gives tier isolation and AZ resilience. The default VPC is a single public-style network; a single subnet has no isolation or resilience.

SNS: a CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric triggers an SNS notification when the threshold breaches — the standard metric-alerting pattern.

Audit logging: console event history is only 90 days and not immutable; app-level logging misses console/CLI calls.

lessons.title: Networking — Core concepts
concepts: NAT gateway: a NAT gateway in a public subnet lets private instances initiate outbound connections while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. A custom VPC with public subnets (load balancers, NAT) and private subnets (app, data) across 2+ AZs gives tier isolation and AZ resilience.

Private subnets: interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) expose services — AWS or SaaS-provider — as private IPs inside the VPC with no internet traversal. Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent throughput for heavy hybrid workloads.
Subnet filtering: the default VPC is a single public-style network; a single subnet has no isolation or resilience.

example.code:
Private subnet instances need
OS patches (outbound HTTPS).
No inbound from internet allowed.
example.walkthrough: A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets private instances initiate outbound connections while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. Internet gateways are bidirectional; VPC peering connects VPCs, not the internet; VPN connects on-premises networks.

pitfalls: Common trap: an internet gateway in the private subnet.
Common trap: a NAT gateway in a public subnet.

lessons.title: AWS SysOps Administrator — Core concepts
concepts: CloudWatch is the operational nervous system: metrics and alarms for thresholds, Logs for centralized log analysis, Events/EventBridge for reacting to state changes, and dashboards for shared situational awareness. EC2 emits basic metrics every 5 minutes; the CloudWatch agent adds memory, disk, and application metrics.

Systems Manager replaces SSH-and-hope fleet management: Patch Manager for OS updates, Run Command for fleet-wide commands, Session Manager for portless shell access, State Manager for configuration enforcement, and Parameter Store/Secrets Manager for configuration and secrets.

Choose deployment strategies by blast radius: in-place is cheapest but riskiest, rolling limits concurrent exposure, blue/green gives instant rollback at double capacity cost, and canary validates with real traffic on a small slice. Database migrations must be backward-compatible regardless of strategy.

Troubleshoot in layers: read the status check pair (system vs instance) before touching anything, check the system log and CloudWatch metrics for evidence, change one thing at a time, and prefer automated runbooks over heroic manual fixes for recurring issues.

Tag everything and centralize: consistent tags power cost allocation, automation targeting, and access control; CloudTrail logs every API call for audit; Config records configuration history so you can answer 'what changed?' during incidents.

example.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name web-cpu-high \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average \
  --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:ops
example.walkthrough: This pages only when CPU averages over 80% for three consecutive 5-minute periods — sustained breach, not spikes. The SNS action routes to the on-call topic. Tune evaluation-periods first whenever an alarm pages too often.

pitfalls: Common trap: alarming on a single datapoint — require consecutive breaches or inherit pager fatigue.
Common trap: assuming EC2 emits disk/memory metrics natively — install the CloudWatch agent for those.
Common trap: using Session Manager without the IAM instance profile — the agent alone is not enough; the role grants the permissions.
Common trap: stop/start as a universal fix — it only helps system-check (hardware) failures, not sick guest OSes.

lessons.title: Cloud Operations on AWS — Core concepts
concepts: Observability is metrics, logs, and traces together: CloudWatch for the first two, X-Ray for the third, with alarms and dashboards turning telemetry into shared awareness. Alert on symptoms (latency, errors) more than causes (CPU).

FinOps is a loop, not a project: tag everything at creation (enforced by policy), review Cost Explorer and CUR regularly, rightsize with Compute Optimizer, schedule non-production off-hours, then commit to the steady remainder with Savings Plans. In that order.

Budgets notify; policies enforce. AWS Budgets with tiered SNS alerts gives humans time to act, while SCPs, tag policies, and Budgets Actions provide actual guardrails — and automated shutdown belongs on non-production, never as a surprise to customers.

Incidents are handled by systems, not heroes: detection via alarms, codified runbooks and SSM Automation for response, blameless postmortems with tracked action items for learning. Every recurring incident is an automation candidate.

Use the Well-Architected Framework as the review cadence: run the Tool per workload, fix high-risk security and reliability findings first, and re-review after significant changes. The six pillars keep optimization balanced instead of lopsided.

example.code:
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics BlendedCost \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE | head -40
example.walkthrough: This pulls last month's cost grouped by service — the starting point of every FinOps review. The top services tell you where rightsizing, scheduling, and commitments will actually move the number.

pitfalls: Common trap: committing to Savings Plans before rightsizing — you lock in a discount on waste.
Common trap: treating AWS Budgets as enforcement — it only alerts; something else must act.
Common trap: alerting on CPU instead of user-facing symptoms — the pager fires while customers are fine, and stays silent while they suffer.
Common trap: skipping postmortems when the fix was fast — the incident will recur until its action items are tracked to done.

simulations.title: The deployment that never finished
simulations.brief: The 14:00 deployment window closed with the new build half-rolled-out: one instance runs the new version, the other still runs the old. Work the evidence before you touch anything.

steps.symptom: Half the fleet runs the new build, half runs the old; the deploy log shows no errors.
evidence:
i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60718  ilb-web-01  running  t3.medium  us-east-1a
i-0f9e8d7c6b5a43210  ilb-db-01   stopped  r6g.large  us-east-1b
options: Re-run the deployment — it probably just needs a second pass
Check whether the deploy targeted the stopped instance and stalled on it
Roll back immediately — a half-deploy is always corrupt
Terminate the stopped instance so the next deploy has a clean fleet
steps.explain: A deploy that stalls on an unreachable target is the classic half-rollout cause. Verify the target set before re-running or rolling back — the old instances may be perfectly healthy.

steps.symptom: The deploy tool waited 30 minutes on ilb-db-01 (stopped) and timed out; ilb-web-01 actually deployed fine.
options: Mark the deploy failed and roll ilb-web-01 back to v3
Exclude stopped instances from the target set and re-run the deploy
Delete the v4 artifact so nobody deploys it again
Extend the deploy timeout to 4 hours and re-run as-is
steps.explain: The artifact is fine and the live host is healthy — the target set was wrong. Fix the targeting (skip stopped instances), then re-run. Rolling back a healthy host adds risk for nothing.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed a stalled rollout by questioning the target set instead of the artifact. Operators fix targeting; amateurs re-run and hope.

simulations.title: Cut over without downtime
simulations.brief: The business demands zero-downtime deploys. Order the blue-green cutover so traffic never hits a half-ready fleet.

steps.context: Blue-green deployment: build the green fleet, verify, switch traffic, retire blue.
items: Shift traffic from blue to green at the load balancer
Deploy the new build to the green fleet
Run smoke tests against the green fleet
Provision the green fleet alongside blue
Terminate the blue fleet after the bake period

simulations.debrief: You ordered the safe cutover: provision, deploy, verify, switch, retire. Traffic moves only after proof — that ordering is the whole discipline.

simulations.title: The 3 AM page
simulations.brief: Your phone buzzes at 03:12: CPU alarm on ilb-web-01. The runbook gives you a decision tree — follow it like the on-call you want to be.

steps.text: The alarm says CPU > 90% for 15 minutes on ilb-web-01. First action?

choices.label: Acknowledge and check whether the alarm is still firing
choices.feedback: Correct — verify current state before acting. Half of all pages self-resolve.

choices.label: Immediately reboot the instance
choices.feedback: Rebooting a production host on an unverified alarm is how outages are born.

steps.text: You rebooted; the alarm cleared but you never learned the cause. The reviewer asks what you should have done first. Answer honestly:

choices.label: Verified the alarm state and gathered metrics first

steps.text: The alarm is still firing and traffic is normal. Next?

choices.label: Scale out — add capacity and investigate the cause in parallel
choices.feedback: Correct: protect the service first (scale), then diagnose. Availability before root cause.

choices.label: Spend an hour finding the root cause before touching capacity
choices.feedback: Wrong priority: while you investigate, users suffer. Mitigate first, diagnose second.

simulations.debrief: You practiced the on-call order of operations: verify, mitigate, then diagnose. Root cause matters — but never more than the users waiting on the service.

simulations.title: The alarm that cried wolf
simulations.brief: The team mutes half their alarms because this CPU alarm pages constantly. Review the alarm definition and click the lines that make it noisy.

steps.config:
Alarm: web-cpu-high
1. Metric: CPUUtilization, ilb-web-01
2. Threshold: > 20% for 1 datapoint (60s)
3. Missing data: treat as breaching
4. Actions: page on-call immediately
5. OK action: none configured

issues.description: A 20% threshold on a single 60s datapoint fires on any brief spike — pure noise.
issues.fix: Raise the threshold (e.g. > 80%) and require N of M datapoints so transient spikes do not page.

issues.description: Treating missing data as breaching pages the on-call every time metrics pause.
issues.fix: Treat missing data as 'not breaching' or 'ignore' for CPU alarms; reserve breaching for heartbeat-style metrics.

simulations.debrief: You found why the team ignores pages: a hair-trigger threshold and missing-data-as-breach. Fix the alarm and the team starts trusting pages again.

sections.heading: Monitoring & Reporting
items: CloudWatch dashboards — provide customizable single-pane views of metrics, alarms, and logs. EC2 publishes hypervisor-visible metrics (CPU, network, disk I/O) by default, but memory and disk-space utilization require the CloudWatch agent installed on the instance.
SNS — a CloudWatch alarm on the CPUUtilization metric triggers an SNS notification when the threshold breaches — the standard metric-alerting pattern.

CloudTrail — CloudTrail logs AWS API activity; enabling it in all regions with log file validation into a restricted S3 bucket gives a tamper-evident audit trail. CloudTrail logs API calls; Config tracks configuration changes — neither monitors disk space.
Audit logging — console event history is only 90 days and not immutable; app-level logging misses console/CLI calls.

CloudWatch Logs Insights — provides an interactive query language purpose-built for searching and aggregating log data at scale. Systems Manager OpsCenter aggregates operational issues as OpsItems from CloudWatch, Config, and other sources, with deduplication and investigation workfl…
Common trap — the CloudWatch agent for memory and disk metrics.
Common trap — increase the CloudWatch alarm period to 1 hour.
Common trap — enable VPC Flow Logs.
Common trap — ask developers to log API calls in the app.

CloudWatch dashboards — provide customizable single-pane views of metrics, alarms, and logs. The EC2 console lists instances without health aggregation; Cost Explorer shows spend; Trusted Advisor shows best-practice checks — none is an ops dashboard.

sections.heading: High Availability
items: Auto Scaling — ALB target group health checks probe the application endpoint (catching app-dead/OS-alive), and Auto Scaling can use ELB health checks to replace such instances. An Auto Scaling group spanning multiple AZs behind an ALB replaces unhealthy instances and rout…
Multi-AZ — RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby and fails over automatically, typically within minutes.
Health checks — instance-level checks only verify the OS; DNS checks don't see app state; scheduled replacement is blind.
Common trap — ALB target group health checks plus Auto Scaling health checks.
Common trap — warm standby with manual failover.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Monitoring & Reporting: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one High Availability lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
